title: Better left said
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez asks how many valuable thoughts go unspoken in any workplace, not the trivial ones but the ideas that could unstall a project, save money, fix a toxic pattern or give staff hours back. She acknowledges why people stay silent: fear of consequences, ego, politics and the unspoken norms that come with a boss. Writing as a leader, she wonders what would happen if the role carried an explicit expectation of drawing out what is going unsaid, especially what many people are thinking. The piece is reflective rather than prescriptive, and its move is to invert the old saying so that some things are better left said.
points: The most costly losses in an organization are the significant ideas and insights people never voice.
People's silence is rational given hierarchy, politics and the unspoken norms attached to a boss.
Part of a leader's job should be explicitly surfacing what is not being said, especially when many people share the same unspoken idea.
Psychological safety is a design target for the leader's own team, even when wider organizational forces limit it.
quotes: But what I’m talking about here is the more significant stuff. The thoughts, ideas, perspectives, and insights that might have the power to really make a difference.

The power to move the needle on that stalled project you know your boss is eagerly waiting for an update on. To streamline a process that will give staff hours of time back each week. To put an end to a toxic pattern you’re seeing with a colleague.
Just imagine what would happen if we let that stuff breathe. If we created a space where these thoughts were encouraged to be out in the open.

As a leader, I get so excited about the possibility of creating this type of space for my team, even if it’s just in our slice of the pie. I also know, at the end of the day, I’m their boss, and there are all sorts of possible weird, unspoken norms at play as a result, but really, does it need to be this way?
What if being a “boss” meant something different? What if being a boss didn’t automatically provoke concealed—or seriously measured—thoughts and ideas, but something different?

What if being a leader came with some kind of explicit expectation that part of the job is to figure out all the insanely valuable stuff that’s not being said, and oftentimes, what’s going unsaid by many? What if this were the norm?
